source.title: Choosing the right basis for interpretability: Psychophysical comparison between neuron-based and dictionary-based representations
source.authors: Julien Colin; L. Goetschalckx; Thomas Fel; Victor Boutin; Thomas Serre; Nuria Oliver

record.tranche_reason: The study compares neuron-based and learned dictionary-based explanations using human judgments of visual coherence, a different measurement of the interpretability claim.
record.gate_note: The study reports human visual-coherence task results for neuron- and dictionary-based representations, plus layer-depth results and an axis-alignment proxy for superposition. It also reports an element-importance check, but that check measures decision relevance rather than polysemanticity. Results cited from prior work are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: Humans judged how visually coherent each unit's top-activating images are, for neuron axes versus matched dictionary directions in ResNet50 and VGG16. This is a different method aimed at whether vision neurons mix patterns, so it bears on V1 indirectly.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is right. Add that the authors find dictionary elements at least as decision-relevant as neurons (Gradient×Input). They attribute the masked ResNet50 advantage to its greater superposition.
record.recipe_differences: Uses CRAFT/NMF dictionary elements and a human psychophysics visual-coherence task in ResNet50 and VGG16, rather than directly cataloging example polysemantic neurons or applying the original sources' analyses.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported task scores vary with representational basis, model, experiment protocol, and layer depth. Experiment II changes stimulus selection to control a semantic confound; the authors say this control only partially succeeds.

fits_no_version.finding: ResNet50's dictionary elements are less axis-aligned than VGG16's (Hoyer 0.40 vs 0.45), which the authors read as more superposition.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: CNN architectures differ in how neuron-aligned their learned dictionary directions are.

fits_no_version.finding: Dictionary-basis coherence rises with layer depth (r=0.35, r=0.38). Neuron-basis correlations are not significant after correction.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The coherence advantage of dictionary over neuron bases grows with depth in CNNs.

record.problems: The study evaluates only two pretrained CNNs and 80 units per model. Visual coherence is a proxy for interpretability, not a direct measure of unrelated response patterns. The authors report that the semantic-confound control only partially succeeds, and note that the results use dictionaries learned from images activating selected neurons rather than full-layer activations.
record.rows_left_out: No claim-relevant results were left out. The element-importance comparison in Section 4.1 was not extracted as a row because it measures decision relevance rather than polysemanticity or visual coherence.

untested.parts: Per-neuron counts of unrelated responses; the specific InceptionV1 examples; whether the mixed patterns share a feature.
Axis alignment is only a proxy; no causal test of capacity pressure.
Initialization, regularization and noise are not varied.
Activation function and regularization are not varied. The ResNet50/VGG16 contrast is two pretrained models with no controlled change and no performance-cost test.
Does not check whether mixed top images reflect one shared feature.
Activation range and scoring method are not varied systematically. The semantic-confound control changes the contrast stimuli only.

missing.what: Cross-model neuron-basis comparison: ResNet50 vs VGG16 shows no difference (z=0.56, p=0.71).
missing.locator: Section 4.3, 'The choice of basis matters'; Fig. 3b
missing.versions: none (possibly V5 context: architecture did not change neuron-level coherence)

missing.what: Cross-model dictionary-basis comparison: ResNet50 85.1% vs VGG16 81.5% (z=2.14, p=0.016).
missing.locator: Section 4.3, 'ResNet50 is more interpretable than VGG16'

record.verdict_notes: Neuron-basis scores are far above chance (about 77–79%), so most sampled neurons look largely coherent at their top activations. This fits V1's 'some neurons' wording but gives no prevalence estimate. The authors say the semantic-confound control only partly succeeded. The neuron-basis rows were reset to cannot_determine because the verdict rests on the paired contrasts.

versions.untested_parts: The study tests visual coherence in sampled ResNet50 and VGG16 units, not the frequency of polysemantic neurons across vision models, the specific InceptionV1 neuron 4e:55, or whether its example inputs share a feature the network uses.
The study does not test transformer language models or token/context responses.
It uses axis alignment as a proxy for superposition but does not test whether excess feature capacity causes polysemanticity.
The study does not test initialization, regularization, or training noise as causes of polysemanticity.

It compares two pretrained CNNs and two representational bases, but does not vary activation function, regularization, or training to measure changes in the share of polysemantic neurons or performance costs.
The study does not establish whether canonical mixed neuron responses are actually one shared feature or related offshoots of one job.

It addresses a semantic confound in stimulus selection, but does not systematically vary activation ranges or explanation-scoring methods to test whether polysemanticity classifications depend on them.

relationships.condition: ResNet50 (Exps I, II) and VGG16 (Exp III), human visual-coherence task on 80 sampled units per model
relationships.reason: Matched dictionary directions were more coherent than neuron axes in all three experiments (r2, r4, r6): 83.5 vs 78.8, 85.1 vs 76.2, 81.5 vs 77.1. This is consistent with some neurons mixing patterns; the evidence is indirect and the gaps modest.
relationships.display_finding: Matched dictionary directions scored as more coherent than neuron axes in all three experiments (83.5 vs 78.8, 85.1 vs 76.2, 81.5 vs 77.1). This fits some neurons mixing patterns, but the evidence is indirect and the gaps are modest.

labels.reason: Dictionary directions beat neuron axes in all three experiments (r2, r4, r6; p<.001, p<.001, p=0.01). This is indirect evidence that some neuron axes mix patterns.

relation.reason: The study's own results compare the coherence of neuron and dictionary bases, which bears on V1 indirectly.

tranche.reason: The study uses a different method: human psychophysics on neuron axes versus matched CRAFT/NMF dictionary directions. The authors frame heterogeneous top images as consistent with polysemanticity, so it aims at whether vision neurons mix patterns.

source_check.notes: Coherence is only a proxy for polysemanticity. Each dictionary was learned on the neuron's top 300 images, and the authors say the semantic-confound control only partly worked. ResNet50 units came from Zimmermann et al. (2023), and Exp II dropped one unit. The axis-alignment result (0.40 vs 0.45) bears on V3 but is not in the rows checked here.

statements.problem: All numbers for this study match the text: 83.5 vs 78.8 (Exp I), 85.1 vs 76.2 (Exp II), 81.5 vs 77.1 (Exp III), 80 units per model, 95% CIs, two models. The 50% chance level is not printed but follows from the two-query forced choice.
The numbers and the model attributions match the text.

reader_labels.reason: Dictionary-based representations scored higher than neuron-based representations in each experiment, consistent with neuron axes being less visually coherent in these tested settings; this is a proxy result, not a direct count of unrelated response patterns (r1-r6).
